newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Red Cross delivers Albania aid, queries U.N. force.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross delivers Albania aid, queries U.N. force.

text.p: A Red Cross truck delivered aid through bandit-ridden Albania without incident on Saturday and the head of the mission wondered if armed escorts from a planned multinational force would help.

The white truck unloaded food at the hospital at Librazhd, a government-controlled mountain town in central Albania, the last stop before Tirana 100 km (60 miles) away after passing through southern regions hit hardest by insurrection on Friday.

"Our operation has gone without problems," said Darcy Christen, the Swiss head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in southern Albania outside the run-down hospital on a hillside in pine trees above the Librazhd.

Three hospital guards holding ageing rifles looked on nonchalantly as workers unloaded sacks of rice, pasta, beans, vegetable oil, jam, potatoes, tea, salt, sugar and detergent from the truck, which came via Greece.
Christen expressed wariness about the decision by the U.N. Security Council on Friday to approve an Italian-led force to help protect humanitarian supplies to the anarchic former communist state.
"This was a successful test case for us. I wouldn't be too happy to have them (a force) with us," he said as sporadic gunfire crackled in the distance.

"But what is fine today may not be so tomorrow," he said, adding that the Red Cross would discuss needs for armed escorts -- relief convoys accepted such protection from warring factions in Somalia or in the breakaway Russian republic of Chechnya.

He said the resolutely neutral Red Cross had set up good contacts in southern Albania, hardest hit by uprisings this month against President Sali Berisha triggered by the collapse of popular savings schemes in January.

Aid workers express concern that the U.N.-approved force, which is to co-operate with Albanian police, could end up identified with Berisha, lose neutrality and become a target for rebels. That might jeopardise rather than help aid.

Italy says any force, which Albania wants to secure ports, Tirana airport and protect aid shipments, would be about 2,500 strong with a similar number in reserve. France, Portugal, Spain, Greece, Turkey, Romania and Austria have expressed some willingness to take part.
Librazhd hospital doctors reckoned they had treated several dozen wounds from bullets and explosives in recent weeks.
In one ward, six-year-old Mario lay sobbing on a bed, his left hand heavily bandaged and blood spattered down his blue woollen trousers as his parents tried to console him.

"He was playing in the yard by the house when he picked up something that exploded," his mother said. Two of Mario's fingers had been blown off by the blast. Doctors said they expected a third finger would have to be amputated.
Doctor Shpetim Qyra welcomed the Red Cross aid. "We've had no food shortages yet, but stocks are running low. Food prices are rising and that makes everything harder," he said.

One metre (yard) cubes of concrete were dumped outside Librazhd, narrowing the road in a makeshift police checkpoint for cars, trucks and horse-drawn carts. In the nearby town of Elbasan, two Chinese-made tanks stood on the main square.

In total, the Red Cross truck is delivering 10 tonnes of food to hospitals, old people's homes and orphanages, including those in rebel-held Gjirokaster and Tepelene. Its final stop will be the port of Durres on Sunday.
"People tell me I'm crazy because I don't get scared," said the truck's driver, Robin Creelman, a Canadian from Nova Scotia.
